WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand electromagnetic shielding (skin depth, aperture leakage, seam and gasket design), how to measure
attenuation in dB with a source and a receiver, and the difference between shielding, filtering, and grounding — the
fundamentals of EMC and hardening engineering.

→the job this maps to: EMC, EMI, and hardening / survivability engineering — defense electronics, aerospace, and
ruggedised-systems teams.
// how it works

Fields stop at a conductor: A conductive shell redistributes charge and induces currents that cancel an external field
inside. At radio frequencies a thin conductive layer is enough — the field only penetrates to the “skin depth,” microns at
GHz.

Apertures leak: Shielding fails at holes and seams, not through the metal. Any gap longer than a fraction of the
wavelength acts as a slot antenna and lets the field in — which is why gaskets, overlapping seams, and fine mesh matter
more than thick walls.
Measuring attenuation: Put a known signal outside (WiFi, a broadcast station, a small legal ISM transmitter) and measure
inside with an SDR. The drop, in dB, is your shielding effectiveness — and every 20 dB is a tenfold reduction in field
strength.
EMP and lightning: A nuclear EMP or a nearby lightning strike is a fast, enormous field pulse. Hardened systems combine

a shielded enclosure with filtered entry points and surge protection, because the shield is only as good as its weakest
cable.

Shield, filter, ground: A complete hardening strategy layers three things: shield the enclosure, filter every wire that
crosses it, and manage the grounding so currents flow around the electronics rather than through them.
▸

[ P R O J E C T 0 1 ]
Faraday Cage & EMP-Hardened
Enclosure
A box that makes a phone go silent — the shielding that protects electronics from EMP and
lightning

$45
beginner
1 weekend
// why this matters

Every piece of defense electronics has to survive an environment full of interference — radar, lightning, hostile transmitters,
and the electromagnetic pulse that hardened systems are built to shrug off. The defense against all of it is the same physics: a

conductive enclosure that stops fields at the boundary. Build a Faraday cage, put a phone inside and watch it lose signal, then
measure exactly how many decibels of attenuation your seams, mesh, and gaskets buy you with an SDR. It is a beginner build
with an unforgettable demo, and it teaches EMC and hardening — the survivability discipline that sits under every ruggedised
system.

// build steps
// interview questions
Build the enclosure

Start with a metal box (or line a box with overlapping foil) and make sure every panel is electrically continuous — check
with a multimeter. Continuity is the whole game.
Test the naive version
Put a phone inside, close the lid, and call it. Watch it lose bars — or not, if a seam is leaking. Note what still gets
through.
Seal the seams
Add copper tape or conductive gasket along every joint and around the lid. Retest the phone; it should now be
unreachable.
Measure attenuation
Set an SDR outside and note a signal’s strength, then put the SDR inside and re-measure. The difference in dB is your
shielding effectiveness. Try it at several frequencies and watch where the box leaks.
Harden a real device

Add a filtered power feedthrough (a feedthrough capacitor or ferrite and cap) and a surge protector so a device inside
can be powered without breaking the shield. Now you have a genuinely hardened enclosure.

survive the field — a Build List field guide
3 / 16

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand subsonic aerodynamics (lift, drag, angle of attack, stall), flow conditioning (honeycombs, screens,
contraction ratio), flow visualisation, and force measurement with a balance. That is the core of aerospace and
aerodynamics engineering, and the wind-tunnel workflow every aircraft program uses.
→the job this maps to: aerodynamics and aerospace engineering — aircraft, drone, and flight-vehicle design and test teams.
// how it works
Lift from pressure: Air moving over a curved wing speeds up and its pressure drops relative to the underside; the pressure
difference integrates into lift. Angle the wing up and lift grows — until the flow separates and the wing stalls.
Conditioning the flow: A fan produces swirl and turbulence. A settling chamber slows the air, a honeycomb straightens it,

fine screens break up turbulence, and a contraction (a smooth nozzle) accelerates it into a clean, uniform test-section
flow.
Seeing the flow: A thin stream of smoke (or fog from a small glycol fogger) introduced upstream follows the streamlines,
making the flow over the wing visible — attached flow, the stagnation point, and the separated wake at stall.
Measuring force: Mount the wing on a sting connected to a load cell (or two, for lift and drag). As the fan runs, the load cell
reads the aerodynamic force directly; plot lift against angle of attack to see the lift slope and the stall.
Reynolds number: The key scaling parameter for aerodynamics. Your small, slow tunnel runs at low Reynolds number,
which changes stall behaviour and lift coefficients — so you report airspeed, chord, and Re with every result.

[ P R O J E C T 0 2 ]
Desktop Wind Tunnel
Smoke lines over a wing and a live lift readout — aerodynamics you can see, on a desk

$80
intermediate
1–2 weekends
// why this matters
Every aircraft, drone, and glider in the defense world was shaped in a wind tunnel long before it flew, and you can build a real

one on a desk. A fan, a settling chamber, a honeycomb flow straightener, a smooth contraction, and a clear test section give
you steady laminar air; add a smoke wand and the streamlines over a 3D-printed wing become visible, and a load cell turns
the invisible force of lift into a number you can plot against angle of attack. It is the flagship of this guide — a genuine
aerospace instrument, visually spectacular, and a hands-on route into aerodynamics and aircraft design.

Why a settling chamber and honeycomb instead of a fan and a tube? A fan produces swirling, turbulent air that would

smear your smoke lines and corrupt any force reading. A settling chamber slows the flow, a honeycomb kills the swirl,
screens break up turbulence, and a smooth contraction accelerates the flow uniformly — which is why real tunnels spend
most of their length conditioning air before the test section.
Why a load cell rather than a spring or eyeballing it? Lift is small (fractions of a newton) and varies smoothly with angle
of attack. A load-cell balance gives a calibrated, repeatable number you can plot to find the lift slope and the stall — the
actual data an aerodynamicist needs. A spring is neither sensitive nor linear enough.
Why does a small tunnel behave differently from a full-size one? Aerodynamics scales with Reynolds number — the ratio

of inertial to viscous forces. A desktop tunnel operates at low Reynolds numbers, so your wing sees “thicker” air, stalls
differently, and produces lower lift coefficients than full scale. Reporting Re with your data is what separates a toy from an
instrument.

// build steps
// interview questions
Build the body

Assemble the settling chamber, honeycomb (a bundle of straws), screens, contraction, and a clear test section, with
the fan at the exit pulling air through. Seal all joints.
Get clean flow
Run the fan and introduce smoke upstream. Adjust screens and honeycomb until the smoke lines through the empty
test section are straight and steady — that is conditioned flow.
Add the wing and balance
Mount a 3D-printed airfoil on a sting attached to the load cell, with an angle-of-attack adjustment. Zero the load cell
with the fan off.
Visualise the flow
Run smoke over the wing at increasing angles of attack and watch the streamlines follow the surface, then separate as
it stalls. Film this — it is the shot.
Measure and plot

Record lift versus angle of attack, find the stall angle, and estimate the Reynolds number from airspeed and chord.
Compare two airfoils. You have run a real aerodynamic test.

6 / 16

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand composite layup (fiber types, weave, stacking sequence, resin), energy absorption and failure modes
(delamination, fiber breakage), instrumented impact testing, and turning a test into data. Materials and structural-test
engineering underpin every protective system in defense.

→the job this maps to: materials and protective-structures engineering — composites, structural-test, and protective-
equipment teams.

!
DROP WEIGHTS, NOT BULLETS
This is a drop-weight impact test, the standard lab method — and it stays that way. Never test panels with firearms or

projectiles: it is illegal outside a licensed range, extremely dangerous, and not what this build is for. Wear eye
protection, keep hands clear of the drop path, and handle composites with gloves and a respirator — epoxy and fiber
dust are real hazards.

SP03 · 31.6 °C · ε 0.95
[ P R O J E C T 0 3 ]
Impact-Resistant Composite Panel &
Drop Tower
Lay up your own protective composite, then hit it with a drop weight and measure what
survived

$70
intermediate
1–2 weekends
// why this matters

Helmets, vehicle panels, and protective gear are built from composites engineered to absorb impact — and the way engineers
develop them is by making test panels and hitting them, repeatably, with an instrumented impactor. Lay up your own panels

from carbon, fiberglass, and aramid with different stacks and resins, then build a drop tower that drops a known mass from a
known height onto them while an accelerometer records the impact. Compare the panels: which cracked, which delaminated,
which shrugged it off. It is hands-on materials engineering with a dramatic slow-motion payoff, and it is exactly how
protective structures get designed.

Composites absorb energy: A composite panel takes an impact by spreading load through stiff fibers and dissipating

energy in the matrix, in delamination between plies, and in fiber breakage. Carbon is stiff, aramid is tough, glass is cheap
and forgiving — and each fails differently.

Layup and stacking: Stacking plies at different angles (0, 90, ±45) spreads strength in all directions, and the order
changes how cracks propagate. Vacuum bagging or careful hand layup controls resin content and voids, which dominate
strength.

The drop tower: A guided mass falls from a set height onto the clamped panel, delivering a known energy (m·g·h). Guides
keep the impact repeatable; a hemispherical impactor concentrates the load like a real strike.
▸

Instrumenting the hit: An accelerometer on the impactor (or a load cell under the panel) records the force-time curve; the
peak force and impulse tell you how the panel responded. Slow-motion video shows the failure as it happens.
▸
Reading the damage: After impact, inspect for cracks, dents, and delamination — tap testing reveals hidden delamination

by its dull sound. Comparing panels at equal energy reveals which layup absorbs best, the data that drives protective
design.

survive the field — a Build List field guide
8 / 16
// build steps
// interview questions
Lay up test panels

Make three or four small panels with different fibers and stacking sequences by hand layup (vacuum-bagged if you
can). Cure fully and cut to identical sizes.
Build the drop tower
Build a vertical guide (tube or rods) with a release at adjustable height and a clamping frame for the panel. Mount the
accelerometer on the impactor. Make the drop repeatable.
Calibrate and dry-run
Drop onto a rigid surface at a known height and record the acceleration to confirm the sensor and timing work.
Compute impact energy from mass and height.
Test each panel
Drop the same energy on each panel, recording the force-time curve and filming the impact in slow motion. Increase
energy on the survivors until they fail.
Analyse and compare

Compare peak forces, inspect damage (cracks, delamination by tap test), and rank the layups. Write up which stack
survived best and why — a real materials test report.

survive the field — a Build List field guide
9 / 16

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand underwater acoustics, piezo transducers and potting, low-noise preamplification, time-difference-of-

arrival bearing estimation, and cross-correlation. Passive acoustic sensing is core to naval, marine, and monitoring
engineering.

→the job this maps to: naval acoustics and underwater-sensing engineering — sonar, marine-monitoring, and ocean-
engineering teams.

!
LISTEN, DON'T DISTURB
This is receive-only. Never build an active (transmitting) sonar — loud underwater sound harms marine life and is
regulated. Keep clear of swimmers and boat traffic, don’t leave gear in the water, and respect wildlife. You are
listening, nothing more.
// how it works
Sound in water: Water carries sound at about 1,500 m/s — four times faster than air — with far less loss, so a boat’s
propeller can be heard kilometres away. That efficiency is why sonar, not radar, sees underwater.

The hydrophone: A piezoelectric element turns pressure waves into voltage. Potting it in epoxy (or oil-filling a rubber
housing) waterproofs it while coupling sound in; a low-noise preamp right at the element lifts the tiny signal before the
cable adds noise.
Listening: Feed the preamp into an audio interface and you hear the underwater world — engines, rain, fish, wakes. A
spectrogram shows the tonals of a propeller (its blade-rate lines) that identify a vessel.

Bearing from two ears: Two hydrophones a known distance apart receive the same sound at slightly different times. That
time difference of arrival, measured by cross-correlating the two channels, gives the angle the sound came from — the
same trick your ears use.
Ambiguity and range: Two hydrophones give a bearing with a left / right ambiguity; three resolve it; moving or multiple
stations can triangulate range. Real towed arrays are just many hydrophones doing this at scale.

[ P R O J E C T 0 4 ]
Passive Sonar Hydrophone Array
Hear a boat before you see it — underwater listening and bearing from a pair of
hydrophones

$50
intermediate
1 weekend
// why this matters
Sound travels farther and faster in water than radio ever could, which is why navies listen. Build a hydrophone from a piezo

element potted in epoxy, drop it in a lake, and you hear propellers, outboards, and the whole underwater soundscape; add a
second hydrophone a known distance away, measure the time difference of arrival, and you get the bearing to the source —

passive sonar, the technique behind anti-submarine warfare and marine monitoring. It is receive-only, cross-disciplinary
(acoustics, transducers, signal processing), and a strikingly different sensing domain from the RF work in the rest of the
series.

survive the field — a Build List field guide
11 / 16

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand ram-air parafoil aerodynamics and control (brake-line steering), guidance to a waypoint from GPS and
heading, closed-loop heading control under wind, and the safety engineering of dropping things — the GNC skill set of
aerial delivery and small unmanned systems.
→the job this maps to: aerial-delivery, small-UAS, and guidance-navigation-control engineering — logistics-systems and
unmanned-aerial teams.

!
CARGO ONLY, AND SAFELY
This carries supplies and nothing else — it is a delivery system and stays one. Drop only in a clear, open area you have

permission to use, never over people, buildings, or roads; keep the payload small and soft; follow your local drone and
airspace rules for whatever lifts it. A self-steering canopy is still a falling object.
// how it works

The ram-air canopy: A parafoil is a soft wing — cells inflated by ram air — that glides, so it can be steered. Pull the left
brake line and the left side slows and dips, turning the canopy left; pull both to flare and slow the descent.
▸
Servo steering: Two small servos on the payload box shorten the left and right brake lines. That gives a controller a
heading command — the whole point that makes the drop precise rather than wherever the wind takes it.
Knowing where you are: GPS gives position; a magnetometer and IMU give heading. The controller computes the bearing
to the landing point and the heading error.
Closing the loop: A heading controller steers toward the landing point, correcting for wind drift, and manages the glide so
it arrives high enough to turn into the wind and flare on the final approach — the same logic full-scale systems use.

The drop platform and safety: The payload is lifted by a drone, a kite, or a safe high point, released to deploy the canopy,
then flies itself down. Everything about the test — area, altitude, payload mass — is chosen so a failure lands harmlessly.
▸

[ P R O J E C T 0 5 ]
Precision Airdrop Parafoil Payload
A parachute that flies itself to the landing zone — self-steering aerial delivery

$90
advanced
2 weekends
// why this matters
Getting supplies to a precise spot from the air is a logistics problem the defense world solved with self-steering parafoils: a

ram-air canopy with servo-pulled control lines and a GPS-guided controller that flies the payload to a coordinate. Build a
small one — a ram-air kite canopy, two servos on the brake lines, a GPS and IMU on the payload box — drop it from a legal
height, and watch it turn toward the landing point and flare. It is aerospace, control, and embedded engineering in one build,
it is pure cargo delivery, and it is one of the most satisfying autonomous systems you can make.

13 / 16

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand environmental test engineering (thermal cycling, vibration, shock and drop), instrumenting a device
under test, designing repeatable fixtures, pass / fail criteria, and reporting — the test-and-evaluation discipline behind
every fielded system.
→the job this maps to: test & evaluation and ruggedisation engineering — environmental-test labs, defense and aerospace
qualification teams.

!
NO BATTERIES IN THE OVEN
Thermal testing means real heat and cold. Never put lithium batteries in the chamber — they can vent or catch fire —

so power the device under test from a bench supply through the wall. Keep chamber temperatures within safe limits,
never use a kitchen oven you will cook in again, and mind the shaker: moving parts and loosened screws fly.
// how it works

The environmental profiles: MIL-STD-810 defines test methods — high and low temperature, thermal shock, vibration,
mechanical shock, humidity, and more — each with a profile of levels and durations matched to the intended environment.
▸
The thermal chamber: An insulated box with a heater (and a Peltier or freezer for cold), a fan for uniformity, and a
thermocouple-controlled loop cycles the device between extremes and holds it there while it runs.
The vibration table: A platform driven by an eccentric motor or a speaker reproduces transport vibration; an
accelerometer on the table confirms the levels and frequencies you are actually delivering.
Shock and drop: A controlled drop from a set height onto a hard surface delivers a mechanical shock; an accelerometer
on the device records the peak g. Repeatable orientation and height are what make it a test rather than an accident.

The device under test: The DUT runs a self-test loop and logs continuously, so you can see exactly when — and whether —
it faulted, reset, or failed during each profile. Pass / fail is defined before the test, not after.
▸

[ P R O J E C T 0 6 ]
Survivability Test Rig
Bake it, freeze it, shake it, drop it — torture-test your electronics to military standards

$85
advanced
2 weekends
// why this matters
Defense hardware has to work after a night at −40, a day in a hot cargo hold, hours of truck vibration, and a drop onto

concrete. MIL-STD-810 is the standard that defines those tests, and you can build a scaled version of the lab: a thermal
chamber that heats and cools, a vibration table driven by a motor or a speaker, and a controlled drop rig, all instrumented,
with the device under test logging whether it survived. Then torture-test something you built and write the report. It is test-
and-evaluation engineering, cross-discipline (thermal, mechanical, electronic), and it turns “I think it’s rugged” into evidence.

Define the test plan

Pick a device under test, decide its intended environment, and set the profiles: temperature extremes and durations,
vibration level, drop height. Write pass / fail criteria first.
Build the thermal chamber
Assemble the insulated box with heater, cooling, fan, and thermocouple control. Verify it can reach and hold your hot
and cold setpoints safely.
Build the shaker and drop fixture
Assemble the vibration table with an accelerometer on it, and a guided drop rig. Characterise the vibration levels you
produce and the drop g’s.
Instrument the DUT
Have the device log a self-test (sensor reads, comms, memory checks) continuously over serial, timestamped, so
faults are attributable to a test phase.
Run the campaign and report

Run thermal cycling, vibration, and drop in sequence, logging everything. Identify failures (which phase, what broke),
fix the design, retest, and write a one-page test report — the deliverable real T&E engineers produce.

The hard part of defense engineering
isn’t the weapon.
It’s surviving the field.

A shielded box, a wind tunnel, an impact panel, a hydrophone pair, a self-steering parachute, a torture chamber for
electronics — six builds from the survivability, aerodynamics, sensing, and logistics side of defense, spanning EE, mechanical,
materials, aerospace, and test engineering. Every one is protective, passive, or logistical. The value is in the discipline: the

shielding, the flow conditioning, the layup, the correlation, the control loop, the test plan. That is what defense and aerospace
teams hire for, across every discipline.
// the skill ladder
Build them in order and each one hands you the technique the next one needs:
shielding →aerodynamics →materials & impact →acoustic sensing →guidance & control →test & evaluation

All six are protective, sensing, or logistics builds — no weapons, no projectiles, no jamming, nothing that harms. Test

panels with drop weights, never firearms. Drop payloads only where it is legal and empty, and never over people. Keep
batteries out of the chamber, keep active sonar off the list, and follow local airspace and safety rules. Build to protect,
deliver, and prove.

DO THIS
Build even one. Film it — a phone going silent in the cage, smoke curling over a wing, a slow-motion impact, a boat’s
bearing sweeping across a plot, a canopy turning toward the mark, a board surviving the chamber — and put the data
and design on GitHub with your test method and an honest write-up. One survivability demo and one clean report
prove you can engineer for the real world.
Full build notes, parts links, and the next field guide go out in The Build List. The people actually shipping these — and
trading layup and tunnel tricks — are in Ohm’s Club.
